sections.b: Sirach 44–50 is a long roll of honor from Israel's past, written about two centuries before the New Testament. Ben Sira, a Jerusalem teacher of about 180 BC, moves from Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob through Moses, Aaron and Phinehas, the judges, the kings and the prophets to Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, then back to Shem, Seth and Adam, and ends with the high priest Simon of his own day. His theme is God's covenants with the fathers and the memory that faithful people leave. The list follows the order of the Torah and the Prophets, and it leaves out Ezra, Daniel, Esther and every woman. Later lists in 1 Maccabees 2:51–60 and Hebrews 11 do something similar for courage and for faith.

common: Sirach 44:1 ('Let us now praise famous men' in the KJV) is the classic text for honoring the faithful dead.

sections.h: Simon son of Onias in Sirach 50
sections.b: Sirach 50:1–21 praises Simon son of Onias, the high priest. Josephus knows two such men: an earlier Simon, son of Onias, who 'was called Simon the Just' (Antiquities 12.43), and a later Simeon to whom an Onias left the high priesthood in the reign of Seleucus, the son of Antiochus the Great (12.223–224). Scholars have identified Ben Sira's Simon, and the Mishnah's 'Shimon the Righteous' (Avot 1:2), with one or the other (Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Simeon the Just'). Ben Sira's Simon repaired the temple, built walls and a reservoir and fortified Jerusalem, which fits Antiochus III's order that the temple work be finished (Antiquities 12.138–141). He describes him coming out 'from the house of the curtain', robed like Aaron, offering at the altar and blessing the people with the Lord's name. The Hebrew of 50:24 prays that the covenant of Phinehas stay with Simon's line; the Greek, made after the family had lost the office, prays for 'us' instead.

Ben Sira (about 180 BC) gives Elijah twelve verses of his hymn (Sirach 48:1–12): a prophet 'like fire' who shut the sky, called down fire three times, raised the dead and was taken up in a whirlwind of fire. He takes up Malachi 4:5–6: Elijah is 'written down' for the times to come, to calm God's anger, turn the heart of the father to the son, and, a task borrowed from the servant of Isaiah 49:6, 'to set the tribes of Jacob on their feet'. Luke 1:17 applies Malachi's words to John the Baptist. Sirach 48:11 is obscure in every witness; it blesses those who saw Elijah.

Sirach 49:10, written about 180 BC, names 'the twelve prophets' together: 'may the bones of the twelve prophets sprout again from their place'. The Greek writes the number as a numeral; the Hebrew manuscript B from the Cairo Genizah (folio XVIII verso, line 15) reads 'and also the twelve prophets' (וגם שנים עשר הנביאים). Ben Sira names them right after Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, the order of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible, and he has just used words of Malachi, the last of the Twelve (Sirach 48:10). Alexandrinus, manuscript B and the Latin go on to say that the twelve comforted and saved Jacob. The verse does not say whether Ben Sira means one scroll of twelve books or twelve prophets remembered as a group.

sections.h: Simon the high priest: Yom Kippur or the daily offering?
sections.b: Sirach 50:5–21 describes the high priest Simon, about 200 BC, coming out 'from the house of the curtain' and offering at the altar. Some read it as the Day of Atonement, the one day the high priest went behind the curtain (Leviticus 16; Mishnah Yoma 5:1); the Yom Kippur poem 'Mareh Kohen' echoes the chapter. Others point out that the details match the Mishnah's account of the daily offering, Tamid 7:2–3: the pieces handed up, the wine poured out, two silver trumpets, the Levites' song, the people bowing and the priestly blessing; the scapegoat and the sprinkled blood are absent. Some see a picture drawn from many services.

Ben Sira gives Aaron seventeen verses (Sirach 45:6–22), far more than Moses: an everlasting covenant, the priesthood of the people, the vestments of Exodus 28, the twice-daily offerings, the blessing in God's name, authority to teach the law, and the firstfruits and sacrifices as income because the Lord himself is the priests' inheritance. Phinehas, 'third in glory', receives a covenant of peace, which the Hebrew calls 'the high priesthood forever' (45:24). Ben Sira sets this beside David's royal covenant (45:25) and blesses the priests of his day (45:26). The section prepares for the portrait of the high priest Simon in chapter 50, who wears the same 'fullness of splendor' as Aaron (45:8; 50:11).

Sirach 45:23–24 ranks Phinehas third in glory after Moses and Aaron, for his zeal in the fear of the Lord when the people turned away at Peor. God gave him 'a covenant of peace', in the Hebrew of manuscript B 'the high priesthood forever'. In the Hebrew of 50:24 Ben Sira prays that 'the covenant of Phinehas' remain with Simon the high priest. A generation later Mattathias launched the Maccabean revolt 'as Phinehas did' (1 Maccabees 2:26), so Phinehas's zeal became a model for armed resistance as well as for priestly loyalty.

Writing about 180 BC, Ben Sira takes 1 Samuel 28 at face value: 'After he had gone to sleep in death, he still prophesied. He showed the king his end and lifted his voice from the earth in prophecy' (Sirach 46:20). The Hebrew manuscript B adds that Samuel 'was sought' after his death. Two centuries before Christ, then, a Jewish teacher treated the speaker as Samuel himself, not a trick or a spirit pretending to be him.

Sirach 48:20–25 praises Isaiah as the prophet through whom God rescued Jerusalem from Sennacherib and turned the sun back for Hezekiah, and adds: 'By a great spirit he saw the last things and comforted those who mourned in Zion' (48:24). The comfort is the language of Isaiah 40:1 and 61:2–3, so Ben Sira credits words from the later chapters of the book to Isaiah himself. Those who hold to one author cite this as an early witness; most critical scholars answer that it shows the book was complete and read as a unity by then, not who wrote its parts.

Ben Sira's Praise of the Fathers (Sirach 44–50) names Zerubbabel, Jeshua and Nehemiah from the return from exile (49:11–13) but never Ezra, though Ezra was the priest and scribe who taught the law, the very ideal Ben Sira describes in 38:24–39:11. Suggested reasons include his focus on builders leading up to Simon (50:1–4), a closer knowledge of Nehemiah's memoir, or reserve about Ezra's ban on foreign marriages. None can be shown. 2 Maccabees 2:13 likewise remembers Nehemiah as a founder, not Ezra.

Sirach ends with an alphabet poem on seeking wisdom (51:13–30), part of which was found in the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a). The speaker sought her from his youth, then invites the untaught: 'Come close to me... and stay in the house of instruction' (51:23; Hebrew 'my house of study'), 'Bend your neck under the yoke' (51:26), 'I toiled a little and found great rest for myself' (51:27). Jesus' words in Matthew 11:28–30 share the invitation, the yoke and the rest. Many Christians read them as Jesus speaking as Wisdom in person; Jewish teachers spoke of 'the yoke of the Torah' (Mishnah Avot 3:5). Whether Matthew draws on Sirach is debated.

uncommon: Some scholars think the alphabet poem of Sirach 51:13–30 was not written by Ben Sira, since it also stands on its own in the Qumran Psalms Scroll.

sections.b: Sirach 51:13–30 was in Hebrew an alphabetic acrostic, each couplet starting with the next letter. The Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11QPs-a, columns XXI–XXII) preserves 51:13–20 and the last words of 51:30, beginning with aleph: 'I was a young man before I went astray' (אני נער בטרם תעיתי). The medieval manuscript B has the poem too, with the letter order broken in places. The Greek, made from Hebrew, cannot show the pattern.

Ben Sira mentions Enoch twice. At the head of the Praise of the Fathers he 'pleased the Lord and was carried off, a pattern of repentance for the generations' (Sirach 44:16; the Hebrew has 'a sign of knowledge'), and near its end 'no one like Enoch was ever made on earth, for he was the one lifted up from the earth' (49:14). The Masada scroll, an ancient copy, has no text of 44:16. Hebrews 11:5 uses the same Greek verb for Enoch being 'carried off'.

sections.h: 'The foolish people who live in Shechem'
sections.b: Sirach 50:25–26, about 180 BC, names three peoples Ben Sira loathes: those on 'the hill of Samaria' (the Hebrew has Seir, Edom), the Philistines, and 'the foolish people who live in Shechem', the Samaritans, whose temple stood on Mount Gerizim. The Hebrew calls them goy naval, the 'nation of fools' of Deuteronomy 32:21. It shows the hostility that Jesus later crossed (John 4:9; Luke 10:33).

sections.h: Job in the Hebrew of Sirach 49
sections.b: The Hebrew manuscript B of Sirach 49:9 says that Ezekiel 'also mentioned Job the prophet, who held to all the ways of righteousness', recalling Ezekiel 14:14, 20. The Greek translator read the Hebrew letters as 'enemy' (אויב for איוב), so Job vanished from the Greek and Latin text, which say that Ezekiel 'remembered the enemies with a downpour'.

Sirach 47:2–11 praises David as the best of Israel, 'like the fat lifted off the peace offering': he played with lions, killed Goliath, broke the Philistines, sang to God with all his heart, set singers before the altar and gave the festivals their beauty. God forgave his sins and gave him 'a covenant of kings'. Ben Sira's David blends Samuel's warrior with Chronicles' founder of temple worship, and 47:22 keeps the hope of a 'root' for David.

The book names its author only at its end. The Greek of Sirach 50:27 reads 'Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem', an odd order that many take to mean Jesus son of Eleazar, of the family of Sira; the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus calls him 'the priest'. The Hebrew manuscript B from the Cairo Genizah has 'Simeon son of Jeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira', and after 51:30 adds: 'Up to here are the words of Simeon son of Jeshua, who is called Ben Sira', and 'The Wisdom of Simeon son of Jeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira'. The Greek manuscripts close with the title 'Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach'. The book ends with his prayer (51:1–12) and his invitation to 'the house of instruction', in Hebrew 'my house of study' (51:23).
